definition: An abnormality of heart rate or rhythm caused by altered cardiac electrical activity; the heartbeat may be too fast, too slow, or irregular.
source_name: American Heart Association — What is an Arrhythmia?

definition: A cardiac rhythm disorder in which abnormal electrical signals make the atria beat irregularly and out of coordination with the ventricles.
A condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs for blood and oxygen.
source_name: American Heart Association — What is Heart Failure?

definition: Injury and death of heart muscle caused when blood flow through a coronary artery is reduced or blocked long enough to deprive the tissue of oxygen.
source_name: American Heart Association — What is a Heart Attack?

definition: Narrowing of the aortic valve opening that restricts blood flow from the left ventricle into the aorta.
source_name: American Heart Association — Aortic Stenosis Overview

definition: Disease of the heart muscle that can make the myocardium enlarged, thickened, rigid, or otherwise impaired and reduce the heart's ability to pump effectively.
source_name: American Heart Association — What Is Cardiomyopathy?

definition: Persistently elevated pressure of blood against the walls of the blood vessels.
source_name: American Heart Association — High Blood Pressure

definition: Heart disease in which coronary arteries cannot deliver enough oxygen-rich blood to the myocardium, commonly because plaque narrows the vessels.
source_name: NHLBI — What Is Coronary Heart Disease?

definition: An infection of the heart's inner lining, most often involving the valves and usually caused by microorganisms that reach the heart through the bloodstream.
A heart-valve disorder in which a valve does not close completely, allowing blood to leak backward through the valve.
source_name: American Heart Association — Heart Valve Problems and Causes

definition: Surgery that creates a new route for blood around a blocked coronary artery by grafting a healthy blood vessel to restore blood flow to the heart muscle.
Coronary bypass surgery performed on a beating heart without using a heart-lung bypass machine.
Surgery used to repair or replace an abnormal or damaged cardiac valve in order to improve the direction and effectiveness of blood flow through the heart.
An operation that treats a weakened or enlarged segment of the aorta by repairing or replacing the diseased portion, using an open or endovascular approach.
Open-heart surgery in which part of an abnormally thickened interventricular septum is removed to improve blood flow in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Surgical removal of part or all of the pericardium, usually to relieve restriction caused by a stiff or diseased pericardial sac.
Surgical implantation of a mechanical pump that helps the left ventricle move blood into the aorta in advanced heart failure.
source_name: Cleveland Clinic — Left Ventricular Assist Devices

definition: Replacement of a severely diseased or failing heart with a donor heart when other treatments are no longer sufficient.
Surgical treatment for atrial fibrillation that creates a planned pattern of atrial scar tissue to block abnormal electrical pathways and guide impulses along controlled routes.
source_name: Cleveland Clinic — Maze Procedure for Atrial Fibrillation

definition: A procedure in which a heart-lung machine temporarily diverts blood away from the heart and lungs, oxygenates it, and pumps it back to the body during surgery.
The moment in the rowing stroke when the oar blade enters the water and the rower begins to apply pressure.
source_name: British Rowing — Glossary of Rowing Terms

definition: The propulsive phase from the catch to the extraction, during which the blade stays in the water and force moves the boat.
source_name: British Rowing — Glossary of Rowing Terms

definition: The phase between the finish and the next catch, when the blade is out of the water and the rower returns toward the starting position.
source_name: British Rowing — Glossary of Rowing Terms

definition: The end of the drive phase, when the handle is drawn toward the body and the blade is prepared to leave the water.
source_name: British Rowing — Glossary of Rowing Terms

definition: The blade orientation in which the spoon is turned parallel to the water, typically used during recovery after extraction.
source_name: British Rowing — Glossary of Rowing Terms

definition: The blade orientation in which the spoon is turned approximately perpendicular to the water in preparation for the catch.
source_name: British Rowing — Glossary of Rowing Terms

definition: A form of rowing in which each rower uses two oars, one in each hand.
source_name: British Rowing — A glossary of rowing lingo

definition: A form of rowing in which each rower handles one oar rather than two.
source_name: British Rowing — A glossary of rowing lingo

definition: The number of complete rowing strokes performed in one minute, usually expressed as strokes per minute.
A pace measure expressed as the time required to cover 500 metres at the current rowing intensity.
source_name: British Rowing — Glossary of Rowing Terms

definition: Degenerative joint disease in which articular cartilage in the knee gradually wears away, causing pain, stiffness, and sometimes bone-on-bone contact.
A tear of one of the fibrocartilage menisci of the knee, often produced by twisting, pivoting, squatting, trauma, or degenerative change.
source_name: AAOS OrthoInfo — Management of Acute Isolated Meniscal Pathology

definition: Damage or tearing of the anterior cruciate ligament, a major stabilizing ligament connecting the femur and tibia within the knee.
source_name: AAOS OrthoInfo — Management of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries

definition: Injury of the posterior cruciate ligament of the knee, commonly associated with a force to the front of a bent knee.
Damage to the ligament on the inner side of the knee that limits excessive side-to-side motion, often caused by a direct blow or twisting injury.
Damage to the ligament on the outer side of the knee that helps control side-to-side stability, typically caused by a force to the inside of the knee.
A localized area of damage to the smooth cartilage covering a joint surface while the remainder of the joint may remain relatively healthy.
A partial or complete tear of one or more rotator cuff tendons that help lift and rotate the shoulder.
A small bone crack caused by repetitive loading when bone breakdown exceeds the body's ability to repair and rebuild the tissue.
Joint inflammation caused by an overactive immune system, producing pain and joint damage and sometimes affecting organs outside the musculoskeletal system.
source_name: AAOS OrthoInfo — Inflammatory Arthritis of the Hip

definition: A chronic disorder of the hair follicle and sebaceous gland characterized by follicular blockage and inflammation.
A chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by sharply defined red plaques covered by scale.
A common inflammatory skin disease characterized by dry skin, intense itch, and recurrent eczematous rash.
A chronic inflammatory condition of the central face commonly causing persistent redness, flushing, visible vessels, and sometimes papules or pustules.
A potentially serious malignant tumor caused by uncontrolled proliferation of melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells of the skin.
An acquired pigmentary disorder in which melanocytes are lost or destroyed, producing well-demarcated areas of depigmented skin.
A skin reaction characterized by transient, usually very itchy wheals, with or without deeper swelling called angioedema.
A benign skin or mucosal lesion caused by infection with human papillomavirus and typically showing a rough keratinized surface.
A superficial dermatophyte fungal infection of glabrous skin that typically produces an annular, scaly, spreading rash.
A chronic or relapsing inflammatory dermatitis affecting sebaceous-rich areas such as the scalp and central face, often with erythema and flaky scale.
The action that starts a rally by sending the ball from the serving side over the net into the opponents' court.
A forearm pass used to control an incoming ball, especially in defense, and direct it toward the setter.
An overhead pass that redirects the ball and places it in a favorable position for an attacker.
A forceful attacking hit that drives the ball over the net toward the opponents' court in an attempt to win the rally.
A front-row defensive action at the net intended to stop or redirect an opponent's attack before it enters the defending court.
The clockwise change of player positions that occurs when a team wins the right to serve from the opponent.
A specialized backcourt player wearing a contrasting uniform whose main role is serve reception and defense and who is restricted from certain front-row actions.
The specialist player who organizes the attack by delivering sets to hitters and choosing among attacking options.
The team's organized first contact after an opponent's serve, intended to control the ball and make an effective set possible.
An attacking action by a back-row player who jumps from behind the attack line before contacting the ball over the net.
The declared denomination, either a trump suit or no trumps, together with the target number of tricks the declaring side undertakes to win.
The player on the side that wins the contract who is responsible for playing both their own hand and the exposed dummy hand.
The declarer's partner's hand, which is placed face up on the table and played according to the declarer's instructions.
A set of four cards, one contributed by each player in clockwise order, won by the highest appropriate card under the rules of the deal.
A card belonging to the suit designated as trumps, which outranks cards of the other suits when legally played to a trick.
The first card played to the first trick of a deal.
The coordinated line of play used by the two opponents of declarer in an attempt to prevent the contract from being made.
A trick won by declarer in excess of the number required by the contract.
A contract requiring at least seven tricks but not enough trick value to qualify as a game contract.
A standard method of evaluating honor-card strength by assigning four points to an ace, three to a king, two to a queen, and one to a jack.
An offence in which a player who was in an offside position when a team-mate played or touched the ball then becomes involved in active play in a prohibited way.
A restart awarded for specified offences from which the kicking team may score directly against the opponents.
A restart from which a goal cannot be scored against the opponents unless the ball first touches another player.
A direct kick from the penalty mark awarded when a defending player commits a direct-free-kick offence within their own penalty area.
A restart awarded to the opponents of the player who last touched the ball when the whole ball crosses a touchline.
A restart awarded when the ball crosses the goal line after last touching an attacker and no goal is scored.
A restart awarded to the attacking team when the ball crosses the goal line after last touching a defender and no goal is scored.
An offence involving prohibited contact between a player's hand or arm and the ball, including deliberate handling or certain actions that make the body unnaturally bigger.
The restart that begins each half and extra-time half and restarts play after a goal, taken from the centre mark.
source_name: IFAB — Law 8: The Start and Restart of Play

definition: A referee-administered restart used when play is stopped and the Laws do not prescribe another specific restart.
source_name: IFAB — Law 8: The Start and Restart of Play
